Hopefully some day in the near future there will be an open-wirebonder project that just accepts g-code like every printer does. In that case, coming from the open.cob to g-code is maybe a week of work with python. 

In the open.cob, there is a section for wire definitions. I have also played around with a python tool to generate these for me from my specifications, but that hasn't worked out completely yet. especially if you want to support all sorts of different loop-forms. I attached a picture of my bonder and ONE of its 3 menues to manage the loop shapes. Unfortunately every bonder that I've worked with so far handles loop-forms differently.
I mean, yeah, they may not take G-code, but they do take something.
Note that loop shape isn't so much the most important here
different tool heads will change what that should be
agree

(for wafer.space)

yeah. I mean, if it's okay to have pins in all directions and they have enough pitch, chip has the same top metallization, wire is always the same and so forth. you can set up the loop form once and it will work. Maybe I focus too much on my own use-case

I'd assume a resin printed or laser sintered COB panel carrier to hold and align the bundles of COBs to be fairly straight forward especially if given to the PCB designer as a template it has to conform to while taking care to properly hug the PCB; then the big part of specifying where the bonding shall go.

can you show when you have a chance what S-Wire is?
By chance?

Generally speaking, an S-loop is a wire-bond loop profile with a longer, relatively flat mid-section between the rise after the first bond and the descent to the second bond. It is used when the span is long, when loop height must stay controlled, when the wire needs extra stiffness against mold sweep, or when clearance over neighboring structures is required.

innermost row is s-shape IIRC

hmm I don't think I understand. can you elaborate?
so one major reason for the large fan out currently is that we don't know the alignment of the die to the PCB traces with enough precision
therefore, we need fairly large PCB side landing pads for the bonds
(much larger than the PCB litho feature size it would reliably offer)
this causes much longer bonds than would be needed otuwise due to limited bond density on the PCB side
Notably, compare the bond pad landing site size to how narrow the escape tracks at the bottom are
The PCB litho could do almost double the density if the alignment would be better
So that the bonds hit both the PCB and the die pads without much widening needed to account for the psoitioning error of the bond movement vs. the pad itself
(this happens from the bonding being referenced optically to the die AFAIK, not to the PCB)

okay, i see.

Which type of glue is used and how much?
Is that specified or does the bonding-company just do whatever they think is correct?

I have placed a lot of dies by hand (which is super annoying) or with this tool: https://elas.hu/en/product/manual-and-semi-automatic-pick-and-place/
I think placing it with +/- 25µm accuracy is possible. what happend to me a couple of times is, that if I added too much glue on the bottom, the chip would drift while the glue hardens

messages.content: Currently it just happens at the bonding co; but I see no inherent issue with not having that be this outsourced.

I wonder if there's no pressure sensitive adhesive suitable for the task; e.g. if I think of the ACF tape that's essentially epoxy prepreg but with no fibers only some loading of nickel spheres that are designed to crush into adjacent surfaces on localized compression letting the rest squeeze out slightly sideways from the pads.

It's heat activated within 10 seconds; but AFAIK it's tacky enough near-instantly.

Like, with that knowledge, I'm confident there's sticky tape or even just using some process that attaches a tacky sheet to the back of the die that can then be placed and pressed briefly before applying hardening.

Or, say, one of the heat activated epoxy types for a few seconds. Or even just having something that can just lay over the area and keep both from sliding away from another, like e.g. just a strip of very soft silicone mat placed across the die being rubbery non-slip against the PCB and the die.

Of course if only we had more free automation of the bonder it could pick up optical alignment from the die and the PCB and just use die coordinates for die bond sites and PCB coordinates for PCB bond sites.

Does that sound right?

Only somewhat connected to what Andrew said above -- I was thinking about it from what type of software might need / use the stuff found in the file and came up with the following items:
 * (a) Python script which generates a nice looking PDF (designed for a human) which can be given to a bond house technician to do the bonding in a manual fashion.
 * (b) Some type of "rules based" DRC checking software which tries to validate if a plan is manufacturable.
 * (c) Some type of "simulation based" DRC checking software which runs a 3d simulation of the bonding head flying over a virtual model of the design and checks for things like clearance between the bond head and other objects.
 * (d) Some type of "bond machine programming" software which loads the data into a wire bonding machine in some way (probably initually using nasty emulated keyboard and screen capture type stuff)
 * (e) Some type of "bond testing / validation" software / board like what @Lauri has developed for wafer.space

I was also thinking there probably needs to be renders of the GDS included so that visual alignment / correction can be done? Ideally this could all work without needing special alignment marks on the part?
Afaik we also want to be able to define how the chip can be electrically tested after bonding. Also render of the die for the bonding diagram

Not generated from the PCB files, but generated FOR the PCB. 
The Die is the source of truth for it's own size and pad placement. From there you can generate "rule based" landingpatterns for the PCB Layout, which also gives you the symbol. The loop-length/shape can be generated from the landingpattern, the die height and pad-placement. Additional parameters for the loops can be generated by inspecting the kicad-netlist + the dies pad-definitions + rules. With a completely filled .cob.json, you can automatically generate bonding program and electrical tests. These give you the source of truth for all further simulation.

Just trying to fit some of @Tim 'mithro' Ansell and @stuart requests are more difficult

the general idea that I implemented was: having all necessary data in one place, so I don't always have to go through a billion documents. my .cob.json file has severd this purpose so far. alle information that is needed can be either extracted from die+process, then you run the half- but well-formed file through a script, that generates the landingpattern on the pcb with some manual intervention (or automatically if you set the correct defaults). 
from there you can generate the wires with some manuel intervention (or automatically if you set the correct defaults). 

The testing specs are something that I added on @stuart s request. I don't know yet how to get them into the file the most convinient way, but it is the correct place to store the information.
as soon as the file is fully-formed, everything else can be generated from there - at least that's what worked for me so far.
and of course the person creating the gds can attach TEXT Records to the pads, which makes all further steps much easier 😉
